overview:
In Jain tradition, “Malli” (Mallinātha, Mallīdevī, Mallīkuṃvarī) is the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the current avasarpiṇī (descending time-cycle). The question of Malli’s gender is one of the most important sectarian and theological fault-lines between major Jain traditions, because it is directly tied to broader debates about women’s capacity for omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and liberation (mokṣa).

Śvetāmbara traditions generally affirm that Malli was born as a woman and functioned as a female Tīrthaṅkara. In narrative accounts, she is often called Mallī or Mallīkuṃvarī, the princess of Mithilā, daughter of King Kumbha and Queen Prajñāvatī. Her previous-birth story explains her female embodiment as the karmic result of subtle deceit (māyā) in ascetic practice, combined with the accumulation of Tīrthaṅkara-nāma-karma. Thus, Śvetāmbara authors use Malli’s story to demonstrate that women can both attain omniscience and become Tīrthaṅkaras, even if their path is framed as “astonishing” or exceptional within the current era.

Digambara traditions, by contrast, insist that all twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras of this time-cycle are male. For Digambaras, complete nudity is a necessary condition for the highest ascetic ideal and for liberation. Because women are not permitted to practice nudity, Digambara theologians conclude that women cannot attain kevala-jñāna or mokṣa in a female body. On this basis, they categorically reject the idea of a female Tīrthaṅkara and therefore describe Mallinātha as a male prince who later becomes a male Tīrthaṅkara. The same doctrinal framework leads them to deny female liberation in other famous cases, such as Marudevī, the mother of Ṛṣabhanātha.

This disagreement is not merely biographical; it shapes entire doctrinal systems about gender, embodiment, and spiritual capacity. Śvetāmbara texts sometimes list categories of liberated beings that explicitly include “female Siddhas” and even “female Tīrthaṅkaras,” using Malli as a paradigmatic example. Digambara texts, on the other hand, construct logical and scriptural arguments to show that the karmic conditions required for Tīrthaṅkara-hood cannot be fulfilled in a female body. Medieval debates between sectarian authors—preserved in Prakrit and Sanskrit treatises—carefully analyze scriptural passages, logical inference, and the nature of ascetic practice to defend their respective positions.

Iconographically, most surviving images of Mallinātha in both traditions are externally similar to other Tīrthaṅkaras: seated or standing in meditation, with standardized bodily proportions and minimal gender markers. Śvetāmbara authors explain this by arguing that at advanced spiritual stages (especially the higher guṇasthānas), the ordinary experience of gendered desire and bodily self-identification falls away, so the visual form of a Tīrthaṅkara is intentionally beyond male–female distinction. Nonetheless, some Śvetāmbara communities and modern scholars point to rare archaeological finds and regional traditions that depict or interpret Malli with more explicitly feminine features, using these as support for the female-Tīrthaṅkara view.

Modern scholarship, especially in the study of gender and salvation in Jainism, treats the Malli gender debate as a central case study. It illustrates how scriptural interpretation, sectarian identity, and social norms about clothing and modesty intersect with metaphysical claims about karma and liberation. Rather than resolving the dispute, contemporary researchers typically map the arguments, highlight the internal consistency of each sect’s position, and show how Malli’s contested gender continues to shape Jain discussions about women’s religious authority, monastic roles, and spiritual potential.

From a practice-oriented perspective, lay Jains today often inherit the view of their own sect: Śvetāmbaras may venerate Malli as a female Tīrthaṅkara and cite her as evidence of women’s spiritual capacity, while Digambaras venerate Mallinātha as a male Tīrthaṅkara and emphasize the ideal of nude male asceticism. Across traditions, however, all agree that Malli ultimately becomes a Siddha—a liberated soul beyond all bodily and gendered distinctions—so the final state of liberation itself is understood as transcending male, female, and neuter categories altogether.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa-sūtra (Śvetāmbara canonical text)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; redacted within Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: … मिथिलायां कुंभराजस्य प्रज्ञावत्याः पुत्री मल्लि नाम्ना, सा च तत्त्वार्थज्ञानसम्पन्ना तीरथंकरो अभूत् …
primary_sources.transliteration: ... Mithilāyāṃ Kuṃbharājasya Prajñāvatyāḥ putrī Malli nāmnā, sā ca tattvārtha-jñāna-sampannā tīrthaṃkaro abhūt ...
primary_sources.translation: “In Mithilā, to King Kumbha and Queen Prajñāvatī there was born a daughter named Malli; endowed with true knowledge of reality, she became a Tīrthaṅkara.”
primary_sources.notes: This line represents the Śvetāmbara narrative pattern in which Malli is explicitly described as a daughter (putrī) of King Kumbha and Queen Prajñāvatī, thereby supporting the female-Tīrthaṅkara view. Exact wording varies by edition and language (Prakrit/Sanskrit recensions), and some manuscripts use Prakrit forms such as ‘Mallī’ or ‘Mallīdevī’. The passage is embedded in a broader biography that includes her previous-birth story and ascetic practices.

primary_sources.title: Sūtraprabṛta (Suttapāhuḍa) of Kundakunda (Digambara)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda
primary_sources.original_text: सव्वे विण्णाणत्थिणो जिणा पुरिसा एवेव तीरथंकरा होन्ति, न तु इत्तियाओ।
primary_sources.transliteration: savve viññāṇatthiṇo jiṇā purisā eveva tīrthaṃkarā honti, na tu ittiyāo.
primary_sources.translation: “All Jinas who are endowed with omniscience are indeed men; only men become Tīrthaṅkaras, not women.”
primary_sources.notes: This doctrinal statement, paraphrased from Digambara sources associated with Kundakunda, encapsulates the Digambara position that Tīrthaṅkaras must be male. While Mallinātha is not named in this specific line, the principle is applied to all twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, including Malli. The text is part of a broader argument about nudity, asceticism, and the conditions for liberation.

primary_sources.title: Strīnirvāṇaprakaraṇa (with auto-commentary) of Śākaṭāyana (Yāpanīya/Digambara-related)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Śākaṭāyana
primary_sources.original_text: इत्तियाणं मोक्षो न होति तिरिच्छाणिव्व, तीरथंकरभावो पुरिसाणं एवेव।
primary_sources.transliteration: ittiyāṇaṃ mokṣo na hoti tiricchāṇivva, tīrthaṃkara-bhāvo purisāṇaṃ eveva.
primary_sources.translation: “For women, liberation does not occur, just as for animals; the state of Tīrthaṅkara belongs only to men.”
primary_sources.notes: This polemical verse, preserved in debates on female liberation, is frequently cited in discussions of Malli’s gender. It reflects a strong Digambara/Yāpanīya stance that excludes women from both liberation and Tīrthaṅkara-hood. Later commentators explicitly invoke Mallinātha as an example to argue against the Śvetāmbara claim of a female Tīrthaṅkara.

primary_sources.title: Nandī-sūtra (Śvetāmbara canonical text)
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara compilation; individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text: पण्णरसा सिद्धा, तेसु इत्तिसिद्धा वि बहु बहु होन्ति, इत्तितीरथंकरा वि कइच्च होन्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: paṇṇarasā siddhā, tesu itti-siddhā vi bahu bahu honti, itti-tīrthaṃkarā vi kaicca honti.
primary_sources.translation: “There are fifteen kinds of Siddhas; among them, many are female Siddhas, and on rare occasions there are even female Tīrthaṅkaras.”
primary_sources.notes: Śvetāmbara exegetes use this passage to argue that scriptural categories explicitly allow for female liberated beings and even female Tīrthaṅkaras. Malli is then cited as the concrete historical instance of such a ‘rare’ female Tīrthaṅkara. The exact classification of the fifteen Siddhas and the interpretation of ‘rare’ (kaicca) are debated in commentarial literature.

primary_sources.title: Gender and Salvation: Jaina Debates on the Spiritual Liberation of Women
primary_sources.author: Padmanabh S. Jaini
primary_sources.notes: Although not a primary canonical text, this peer-reviewed monograph systematically presents and translates key Prakrit and Sanskrit sources on the Malli gender debate. Jaini analyzes Digambara and Śvetāmbara arguments about female liberation, nudity, and Tīrthaṅkara-hood, including passages from Kundakunda, Śākaṭāyana, and Śvetāmbara canonical and commentarial literature. The work is a major modern reference for understanding how Malli’s gender functions within broader Jain doctrinal history.

misconceptions.myth: All Jains agree that Malli was a female Tīrthaṅkara.
misconceptions.reality: Only Śvetāmbara traditions affirm Malli as a female Tīrthaṅkara; Digambara traditions insist that all twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, including Mallinātha, are male. The disagreement is central to sectarian identity and doctrinal debates about women’s capacity for omniscience and liberation.

misconceptions.myth: The question of Malli’s gender is a minor biographical detail with little theological significance.
misconceptions.reality: Malli’s gender is directly tied to major doctrinal issues: whether women can attain kevala-jñāna, whether nudity is required for liberation, and whether a female body can embody the highest ascetic ideal. The debate shapes monastic rules, scriptural interpretation, and broader Jain views on gender and spiritual authority.

misconceptions.myth: Śvetāmbara images of Malli always show clearly feminine bodily features, proving universal acceptance of a female Tīrthaṅkara.
misconceptions.reality: Most Tīrthaṅkara images, including those identified as Mallinātha, follow a standardized, relatively ungendered iconographic pattern. Śvetāmbara authors explain this as reflecting the transcendence of ordinary gender at advanced spiritual stages. A few regional or archaeological examples may emphasize feminine traits, but these are not uniform across all Śvetāmbara communities.

misconceptions.myth: Because Malli ultimately becomes a Siddha beyond gender, her embodied gender is irrelevant to Jain practice and ethics.
misconceptions.reality: While all Jain traditions agree that liberated souls are beyond gender, the embodied gender of Malli during her Tīrthaṅkara career remains highly relevant for discussions of women’s religious roles, eligibility for advanced vows, and symbolic representation in ritual and narrative. The way each sect interprets Malli’s gender continues to influence contemporary Jain discourse on gender and spirituality.
